extracted.intended_audience: policy researchers, political economists, regulatory scholars, and policymakers interested in financial regulation and interest-group influence on rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Quantitative and case-based evaluation of how publicly traded banks' participation in administrative rulemaking (comments) correlates with firm-level market gains and regulatory changes, using intra-day event-study methods and focused case studies (Volcker Rule, debit card interchange fee).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commenting participation in rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: The commenting activity of financial entities in Dodd‑Frank related rulemaking at the Federal Reserve (i.e., whether a bank participates by filing comments during rulemaking).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use submitted comment participation as a binary or graded indicator of engagement in rulemaking; compare participants against nonparticipants to assess differential outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intra‑day event‑study measurement of market reaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Using intra‑day event‑study methods to analyze market reactions around rule announcements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement high‑frequency (intra‑day) event windows around rule announcements to detect immediate market responses attributable to rule-related information; this is the primary empirical method for linking rulemaking events to asset price movements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favorable market reactions associated with participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Favorable market reactions around rule announcements that are associated with participation in rule‑making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret positive abnormal returns around announcements for commenting firms as evidence consistent with influence; assess statistical significance and robustness versus nonparticipants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Percentile ranking of asset price returns for commenting banks
rubrics_metrics.description: In response to a rulemaking event, and compared to nonparticipants, commenting banks obtain asset price returns at the 55th to 62nd percentile of ranked returns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use percentile-ranking of firm returns (e.g., 55th–62nd percentile) relative to an appropriate benchmark distribution to quantify how commenting firms fare versus peers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregate excess returns attributable to participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Observed Federal Reserve rulemaking participation by publicly‑traded banks accounts alone for $7 billion in excess returns in the post‑Dodd Frank era.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggregate firm‑level abnormal returns over the relevant sample to estimate total dollar value benefits to industry from participation; report period bounds (post‑Dodd‑Frank era) and attribution assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case‑study linkage between comments and rule changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Closer examination of two rules—Volcker Rule and the debit card interchange fee rule—suggests that these valuations are driven by changes in rules moved by comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complement event‑study evidence with detailed case studies that trace comment content to subsequent rule changes to strengthen causal inference that comments influenced regulatory outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mobilization of legal expertise as a mechanism of influence
rubrics_metrics.description: The differential ability of interests to mobilize legal expertise is a dimension of political inequality that helps explain industry influence in rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess differences in access to and use of legal expertise (e.g., lawyer involvement, quality of legal argumentation) across commenters as a mediating variable for influence; consider measuring legal capacity or counsel engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: New measures of industry influence in regulatory politics
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishing new measures of industry influence in regulatory politics, especially in rulemaking, by combining participation and market‑impact indicators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct composite or multiple complementary metrics (participation indicators, abnormal returns, aggregate dollar impacts, and case evidence) to capture industry influence more fully than single indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and context: Dodd‑Frank era Federal Reserve rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: The empirical analysis focuses on Dodd‑Frank related rulemaking at the Federal Reserve in the post‑Dodd‑Frank era.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit inference and measurement frameworks to the institutional and temporal scope of the study; recognize that results may be specific to Federal Reserve rulemaking and the post‑Dodd‑Frank regulatory environment.
